claim: This project seeks to make a conceptual contribution to this discussion through a clear framework or concept capable of holding these perspectives together, offering a usable shared vocabulary that may be adopted by states and by those working with them in international fora.

The research will also consider what such a framework implies for the design of international institutions and coordinated measures that would be needed to act on what these states say they want, and is likely to have a strong AI middle-powers focus.

The core problem is therefore one of incentive alignment: rigorous safety audits are dependent on deep access granted by the frontier labs; yet those labs will grant deep access only if they (and their auditors) can trust that fulsome, AI-assisted audit records will not inadvertently become evidence (at scale) against them in court.
evidence: Third-party safety audits are becoming the de facto mechanism for safeguarding frontier AI development. They are a feature of nearly every AI safety governance proposal, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's recent call to embed outside evaluators inside frontier labs.

Given the scale and complexity of the models under review, third-party auditors must increasingly rely on AI tools of their own. Yet as frontier labs face increasing litigation following AI incidents, these machine-generated audit records are becoming critical evidence that could help establish products liability. And while a human auditor's communications with the lab's counsel might be shielded from disclosure, the underlying (and far more valuable) AI-generated records are likely to be treated as ordinary business records that could be subpoenaed in later litigation. This creates a perverse incentive for frontier labs to limit the deep, non-public access a rigorous audit requires, and can have a chilling effect on auditors from fully documenting their important deliberations.

claim: This project seeks to adapt that risk-modelling methodology to AI-enabled harmful manipulation with a focus on the political domain, such as influence operations targeting elections or public debate.

The primary output will be a research pre-print or policy report describing a part or whole of the set of political manipulation risk models and a shorter accessible piece summarizing key takeaways from our research.
The project will turn these lessons into concrete threshold design principles: The quantity measured, the trigger level, who sets it, and how it varies by agent archetype and context.
evidence: A set of candidate observables such as behavioural clustering and divergences, feedback loops, and behavioural drift will be proposed against which escalation can be assessed and thresholds proposed.

claim: The primary output is a working paper or preprint for technical and policy audiences, with a short-form version for a tech-policy venue.
This project will examine what different early warning signs actually tell an organisation and what further information is needed before different responses are appropriate.

The work will be grounded in examples drawn from high-consequence settings (for example finance, healthcare, energy or critical national infrastructure), where uncontained propagation has a plausible route to systemic harm.

The team will review the available technical research and any operational documentation that exists, drawing on incident-response practice from adjacent domains (cybersecurity, financial operations, industrial control systems) where direct evidence from agentic deployments is not yet available.

The project will not develop a new detector or prescribe universal numerical thresholds; the main output will be a research paper with a practical supplementary table linking warning evidence to possible responses, their requirements and the responsibilities involved.

This project aims to identify the gap between the capabilities required for handling an advanced AI crisis ("the capability target") and the capabilities governments currently hold ("current capability").
It picks up from a previous AI Governance Taskforce cohort project and focuses on substantiating the capability target through a Delphi study with subject-matter experts (SMEs).
Governments have yet to apply this thinking to advanced AI; this project is a step towards doing so.
evidence: Governments have faced "deep uncertainty" before. Certain defence, flood and financial supervisory policies no longer prepare for a single predicted future but build capabilities that protect across many. This works because capabilities remain definable even when accurate risk assessment is impossible.
